patterns: INVALIDATION LEVELS ARE SET BUT NEVER ENFORCED. MSFT's 5/19 entry set 'stock closes below $400' as its stop; MSFT closed below $400 on 6/10 and fell to $352 by 6/25 without a single session flagging the breach. A second, self-imposed trigger set on 6/17 ('$380 break-below = trim') was breached on 6/24-6/25 and also never acted on. This is the single most concrete, fixable failure in the whole history: research is genuinely updated with fresh data every session, but the stated triggers from prior sessions are never checked against current price before deciding to hold again.

Catalyst-anticipation trades lose money twice in the same way: AAPL was built up over two weeks purely ahead of WWDC on Street-high analyst targets, then closed at a loss when the event disappointed (-4.4%). XLE was bought on an Iran/Hormuz war-shock narrative and invalidated within 6 days by IEA demand data (-5.2%). Both are 'buy the well-telegraphed catalyst, thesis already priced in, event undershoots' failures.

Whipsaw churn between QQQ and AAPL: bought 1 QQQ (5/28), sold it 6 days later to fund more AAPL (6/3), then closed all of AAPL and bought QQQ again (6/16) -- three moves between the same two vehicles in three weeks, netting a modest loss overall once the AAPL leg is included.

Concentration risk was well-managed early (NVDA trimmed from ~45% to ~34% of equity across two sessions in late May) but that discipline was never reapplied after 6/2, even as new fundamental risks emerged on both MSFT (capex/FCF compression) and NVDA (China market exit) through June.

The single unmanaged, un-researched position (SPY, held flat for 45 sessions) outperformed every actively-managed name and the whole book. The portfolio's entire active management layer has subtracted value relative to just holding the passive core.
suggested_adjustments: Make invalidation checks mechanical, not narrative: every session must explicitly compare current price to any invalidation/trigger level set in a prior session for each open position, and if breached, the default action is trim/close -- not a fresh 'thesis still intact' paragraph. This alone would have caught both MSFT breaches.
If a position is down >15% from entry AND has breached its own stated trigger, require an actual size reduction before the position is allowed to just 'hold' again in the next session.

Discount well-telegraphed catalysts (WWDC, COMPUTEX, earnings) that are already reflected in raised analyst price targets going into the event -- require the outcome to beat the re-priced expectation, not just occur, before sizing into it. This would have blocked the AAPL WWDC add.

Stop rotating capital between overlapping vehicles (QQQ vs. direct mega-cap names) to fund a different conviction trade -- pick single-name or broad-ETF exposure per thesis and hold it, rather than swapping mid-stream.

patterns: WORST relative-performance window in the journal's history: portfolio +1.40% vs SPY +4.01%, VT +4.09%, SSO +7.69% (alpha vs SPY -2.61pp) -- a sharp reversal from the prior window's rare positive-alpha result. The stop-then-2-session-reconfirm cycle on SPY is now visibly expensive, not just theoretically so: closed 7/30 near breakeven on the $735 stop, then had to wait through 8/3-8/5 for a fresh SMA crossover to hold two full sessions before re-adding on 8/6 -- by which point SPY had already run from ~$738 to ~$771 (+4.5%). The rule correctly prevents chasing a fresh high from a flat start, but does not distinguish that case from re-entering after being stopped out of a position the account already believed in days earlier.

Fast-moving geopolitical/macro catalyst trades keep losing money on the same pattern: the June XLE entry, the AAPL/WWDC add, and now the 7/23-7/27 XLE re-entry (bought on a Brent breakout above $94, closed 4 sessions later at -2.5% when the escalation reversed) are three separate instances of sizing into a headline-driven catalyst that reverses within days. Exit discipline has been consistently good on all three; entry timing/sizing on this category of trade has not.

NVDA concentration risk -- the single most-repeated complaint across the last three weekly reviews -- was decisively fixed this window via two deliberate trims (7/20 and 7/28), taking the position from ~32.8% of equity down to ~12%. This is the clearest process win of the period and should be locked in as the template: trim on strength/ahead of a dated catalyst, not only on a hard stop breach.

The orphaned-git-branch infrastructure bug flagged in four consecutive prior reviews has not been fixed: sessions on 2026-07-24 and 2026-08-01 both discovered and had to manually recover journal entries (07-22, 07-23, and 07-31 respectively) stranded on branches that never merged to main. This keeps costing session time and risks a future session silently missing prior-day context if the recovery step is ever skipped.
suggested_adjustments: Distinguish 're-entry after a stop-driven exit' from 're-entry after sitting flat' in the SMA-confirmation rule: if a position was closed on a mechanical stop and the signal flips back favorable within a few sessions, allow a single-session reconfirmation before re-adding rather than the full 2-session bar designed to stop chasing fresh highs from scratch -- the current rule cost ~4.5% of missed SPY upside this window.

Cap position size on headline-driven geopolitical/macro catalyst trades (Iran/Hormuz-style XLE entries, event-driven single-name adds) at a lower ceiling -- e.g. <=5% of equity -- until the catalyst has held for 2+ sessions without reversal; this category (June XLE, AAPL/WWDC, July XLE) has a 0-for-3 record in this journal.

Add an explicit weekly cash-utilization check: the account held roughly 40-60% cash for multiple sessions this window ($5,668 of $9,494 equity as of today) while SPY and MSFT both ran hard without full participation. Require each session to note whether elevated cash reflects a deliberate risk-off stance (e.g., waiting out FOMC/NFP) or simply an absence of new signals, so it's a decision rather than a default.

Escalate the branch/merge infrastructure bug beyond another journal note -- this is the fourth consecutive weekly review flagging it, two more sessions had to self-heal it this window alone, and the risk of a silent continuity break grows every time it recurs unfixed.
summary: Review window 2026-07-17 to 2026-08-07 (18 sessions). Portfolio +1.40% vs SPY +4.01%, VT +4.09%, SSO +7.69% -- the worst relative-performance window in the journal's history, driven not by bad picks but by a risk-averse posture (NVDA cut from ~32% to ~12% of equity across two trims, SPY fully out of the market for 5 sessions after a mechanical stop, MSFT held modestly) that missed the summer's strongest rally (record highs on Big Tech earnings plus a surprisingly dovish read on a very weak July NFP print). The two NVDA trims finally fixed the concentration risk flagged in three straight prior reviews -- a genuine process win -- but the SPY stop-out/reconfirm cycle and a third failed geopolitical-catalyst trade (XLE, -2.5%) show the current rulebook has real, quantifiable costs alongside its benefits. MSFT's disciplined post-earnings re-entry (+10.4%) was the standout decision of the window. The orphaned-git-branch bug remains unfixed for a fourth straight review.
